checkpoint.measure: Score share against fixed practice opponents (0.5 = even)

tiers.label: Practice player = the strongest program (our best)

skills.name: Stays on its feet in play
skills.real: The HSL lists dynamic walking as a core problem; the most common action before a goal is a sprint. A humanoid that falls in contact leaves its team short.
skills.measure: the match record: own falls / (robots × match minutes). Gate: ≥ 2 robots walking (replay).

skills.name: Stays up when pushed
skills.real: Body contact happens in play (pushing has a legal limit). Standing after a knock reads 'staying up in contact' directly.
skills.measure: Scenario push: every 15 s of play each standing own robot gets a 0.8 m/s sideways push at its trunk (alternating); share not down within 3 s. Gate: the team walks (≥ 10 m per minute).

skills.name: Walks in play
skills.real: Positioning and turning come before any kick. A standing team does nothing.
skills.measure: Replay / scenario trace: own robots' travel while standing (placements excluded), metres per minute.
skills.line: ≥ 2 robots at ≥ 6 m per minute in 2/3 of matches

skills.name: Gets up after a fall
skills.real: The HSL requires robots to recover alone; 20 s without an attempt means removal. The real T1 gets up in 2.7-2.9 s.
skills.measure: Match: the match record / falls (pooled, ≥ 3 falls). Scenario getup: three times in play every own robot is laid down in the rules' standard supine pose (≥ 1.2 m from the ball); time until it stands ≥ 1 s.
skills.line: Match ≥ 80 %; scenario: up within 20 s after ≥ 2/3 of the lay-downs

skills.name: Not sent off for staying down
skills.real: HSL: no attempt to get up within 20 s means removal, and the team plays short.
skills.measure: the match record incapable = 0. Gate: ≥ 3 falls.

skills.name: Keeps the ball in view with the head camera
skills.real: Champion teams locate ball and players by vision. With only a head camera, a ball out of view has to be searched for by moving the head.
skills.measure: Replay / scenario trace: in play, the share of own robots on the pitch with the ball inside the head camera frustum (80 × 96 deg, no occlusion). Scenario search: the ball put at rest 2 m behind A2; time until A2 first has it in view.
skills.line: Match ≥ 0.75; scenario: in view within 5 s in ≥ 2/3 of trials

skills.name: Finds and touches the ball
skills.real: After seeing the ball, the robot walks there and plays it.
skills.measure: Match: own touches in the match record. Scenarios search / loose: trials where an own robot touches the ball before the opponents.
skills.line: Match ≥ 20 a match in 2/3 of matches; scenario: first touch in ≥ 1/2 of trials

skills.name: Reacts to the ball in time
skills.real: A whole team 200 ms slower loses 0.92 goals a match (card hslc4). When the ball moves, the nearest player has to move at once.
skills.measure: Match replay: after a kick, time until the nearest own robot moves towards the ball faster than 0.3 m/s, median. Scenario loose: a ball rolled at 2 m/s from near the centre circle into the own half; the same reading.
skills.line: ≤ 1.0 s median in 2/3 of matches / ≥ 2/3 of trials

skills.name: Control loop keeps commanding
skills.real: Real teams train gaits and kicks with RL and run a control loop that commands on time. A stalled loop leaves the robots uncontrolled.
skills.measure: Command rows of world/the match log: the gap between successive commands per own robot, p99 in steps. Gate: ≥ 2 robots walking.

skills.name: Passes
skills.real: Tactics are one of four performance factors; in this simulator everyone chasing the ball is the strongest known play, so it stays secondary.

notes.challenge: Three humanoids a side, built up from the joints. The program walks each robot, finds the ball with a head camera it has to aim, and must get a fallen robot up by itself before it can play again.

achieved.text: Claude Opus 5.5 waited out untaken kick-offs for the legal 10 s and shot from the centre spot: 29 of its 87 goals started there, 24 of them in three matches against DeepSeek and GLM.
In HSL2-F18 Gemini 4 Argon led 2:0 from restart routines that drew Opus position penalties; Opus deployed three restart fixes and scored the next three goals.
All five goals GPT-6 Astra conceded in HSL2-F17 were last touched by its own robots, the keeper on four; two count as own goals, three as Gemini shots deflected in.
Opus's robots fell 3.9 times a match by the world's incident count, Astra's 19.4 and Kimi 3.1 Pro's 48.

Claude Opus 5.5: Trained a learned kick before its second Championship match: its on-target kicks went from 1.4-2.4 m/s in fresh Open Arena matches to 5.3-6.9 m/s from 7-10 m.
Gemini 4 Argon: Learned to get up between matches: 4 of 15 falls recovered in its first Championship match, every fall in matches 2 to 6, while its fresh Open Arena programs never got up.

interface.sees: One head camera per robot (480 × 360, a new frame every 20 ms), each robot's joints, balance sensors and position on the field, and the referee's calls. The ball and the opponents appear only in the camera images.
interface.controls: A target angle for each of the 23 joints of all three robots, every 20 ms, in real time. Walking, kicking, aiming the head and getting up after a fall are all the agent's own programs.
interface.moment: Final, Gemini 4 Argon v Claude Opus 5.5, level at 2–2 in the second half, 20:39 in the replay. Opus's robot 2 (red, ringed) has just struck the winning goal. Its head camera, in the frame its program received, shows the ball heading past Gemini's defender toward the goalkeeper.
details: Cameras: one in each robot's head, 480 × 360 pixels, 80° vertical field of view. The camera turns with the two head joints, so the program aims it. Each camera takes a frame every 20 ms; the newest frame a program can fetch is 40 ms old, stamped with its step.
Own robots: joint angles and speeds, trunk orientation, gyro and accelerometer, trunk height and speed, position and heading on the field, and whether each robot is down, getting up or penalised.
Referee: score, half, clock, kick-off, every robot's penalty, the penalty shoot-out, and events such as goals, balls out and fouls.
Not given: where the ball and the opponents are. The programs find them in the camera images.

Commands, per robot: a row of 23 joint targets for the next 20 ms step; a plan of up to 50 rows (one second) from a chosen step; or hold the current row. Commands for several robots sent together act on the same step.

How a command moves the robot: targets are clipped to the joint ranges, then a fixed PD controller runs every 5 ms behind a 20 ms actuator delay, then the vendor's motor torque and speed limits apply.
Timing: the match runs at real speed and never waits for the agent. A command acts at the next 20 ms step; physics runs every 5 ms; a match lasts about 30 minutes.
No ready-made skills: balance, walking, turning, kicking and standing up are built by the agent. A fallen robot returns to play only after it gets up by itself.
Before kick-off: 2 hours of preparation with a full practice copy of the match world, a practice opponent and a GPU training kit. Programs can be updated during the match too.
